rationale: B wins because it has sharper assignment anatomy and better proof gates: "payments-infrastructure trade reporter covering card issuing, BIN sponsorship, local licensing, and cross-border settlement" is a real sub-beat, not a vague fintech bucket. A is strong, but "Brex spends big on global infrastructure without saying if it's profitable" turns an undisclosed cost question into a premise. That is a fishing expedition wearing a headline.
gaps_in_A: "Brex spends big on global infrastructure without saying if it's profitable" invents the "spends big" premise. The update gives valuation and undisclosed profitability, not buildout cost, burn, or spending level.

"cards and local-currency reimbursement live in 50 countries at once, not a phased pilot" overstates what is supplied. The facts say launching in 50 countries; they do not prove every country is live simultaneously.
"expense software has to go everywhere its customers do" is a decent trend frame, but it leans on one company launch until the comparable-vendor proof exists.
A misses the cleaner payments-plumbing angle: who issues the cards, which partners or licenses are involved, and how local reimbursement actually settles.
gaps_in_B: "The finance team that stopped wiring reimbursements across borders" invents the before-state. The update says local reimbursement; it does not say customers were wiring reimbursements before.
"the wires, the FX losses, the month-end mess" decorates an evidence hole. Good reporter bait if proven, sloppy if pitched before a named customer confirms it.
"the startup card company" leans on positioning not fully supplied by the update. The facts say Brex serves many venture-backed startups, not that the market currently sees it only that way.
"card issuing, BIN sponsorship, local licensing, and cross-border settlement" is the right infrastructure territory, but B must keep those as questions until Brex confirms the actual plumbing.
